claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colony microstructure.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and is brittle.
Significant dislocation accumulation or pile-ups occur at internal lamellar boundaries in the untreated alloy.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries generate local stress concentrations that contribute to microcracking and catastrophic damage.
A trace addition of a ductilizing element such as Cu will preferentially segregate to the lamellar phase boundaries.
A subsequent optimized annealing treatment will enhance dopant segregation at the phase boundaries.
Dopant segregation chemically modifies the lamellar interfaces.
Dopant segregation reduces the barrier for dislocation motion at internal phase boundaries.
The reduced interfacial barrier enables smoother dislocation transmission across lamellar interfaces.
Smoother dislocation transmission alleviates local stress concentrations associated with dislocation pile-ups.
Alleviating pile-ups and stress concentrations decreases microcrack formation and catastrophic damage during straining.
The doped and annealed alloy will have greater tensile elongation to failure than the untreated alloy.
The doped and annealed alloy will maintain or slightly increase its yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The doped and annealed alloy will maintain or slightly increase its ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The intervention's effectiveness depends on achieving sufficient and spatially uniform dopant segregation.
Non-optimal dopant concentration or annealing conditions may fail to overcome the dislocation pile-up problem.
The proposed comparison is to be performed under room-temperature, quasi-static tensile loading at approximately 10^-3 s^-1 in standard laboratory conditions.
